title: Leaked Mass Effect 5 trailer is being "re-scored" by one of the original trilogy's composers, so folks can get a taste of his musical vision for the game
author: Mark Warren
content:
More Massively Effective tunes incoming

One of the composers who contributed to the scores of the original Mass Effect trilogy has decided to re-soundtrack the Mass Effect Universe trailer which leaked following the game's cancellation and BioWare's closure. Sam Hulick's aim, aside from making this year's N7 Day a tiny bit less depressing if he can deliver as planned, is to share some of his "musical vision" for the RPG.

Hulick announced his plan on BlueSky, having already started working on a new score for the trailer "for no reason other than closure". "My plan is to release the re-scored Mass Effect Universe trailer for N7 Day," he wrote. "A little tight, since I'm a bit busy pitching for a new game, but I'll see what I can do! I don't wanna rush it, and I want it to properly represent my musical vision for MEU."

With composer Austin Wintory having recently released a collection of tunes he put together while in talks to potentially work on a proper soundtrack for what would have been the fifth Mass Effect game, Hulick's efforts will mean there are two different takes on what Universe might've sounded like out there in the wild. It's somewhat of a silver lining to the dark cloud of the game's demise. You can rightly argue that any canned game tends to be eulogised in terms that point to it having had the potential to be the best thing since sliced bread in a fashion that perhaps over-eggs the pudding a bit, but it's always interesting to learn what those who did or could have worked on such games had in mind.

Having takes on Universe's soundtrack from both Hulick and Wintory out there certainly isn't hurting anyone. The former's also offered his view on the ongoing community-driven efforts to pressure EA into not putting the series on ice, as they have the likes of Burnout in the past. "What really sucks & cannot be undone is all the folks at BioWare who lost their jobs," he wrote. "Even if EA licensed the IP, that doesn't solve anything for them. Someone with a lotta cash would have to license it AND hire the team."

Pending that sort of miracle, the likes of the trailer, these tunes, and other details ex-BioWare devs have shared about what the studio hoped to achieve with Universe are at least meaning fans aren't entirely left in the dark about the work going on during BioWare's final chapter.

title: It usually takes Shipment a lot longer to arrive in Call of Duty, but it's coming to Modern Warfare 4 today, just four days after launch - a new record for Call of Duty
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Crate expectations.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is getting a small update today that includes the latest iteration of Infinity Ward's iconic Shipment map. The map arrives just four days after Modern Warfare 4's launch last Friday, 23rd October, which is unusually quickly.

Shipment is the original Call of Duty 'small map'. First introduced in Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare in 2007, the map is designed to offer a breakneck pace of combat no other multiplayer map could. Though there have been Shipment-like small maps over the years - chiefly Treyarch's infamous Nuketown in the Black Ops sub-franchise - nothing could quite replicate Shipment's dizzying rhythm of mayhem.

Shipment's arrival in Modern Warfare 4 was expected, of course; the developer even announced the 27th October release date in a blog post prior to launch. However, joining the roster so close to the game's launch is notable.

Shipment typically arrives two or so weeks post-launch, usually in a game's first live service season. It's been part of Modern Warfare 2019, Modern Warfare 2 (2022), and Modern Warfare 3 (2023). A few other COD titles have versions inspired by it, though not entirely identical, such as COD: WW2's Shipment 1944.

It's long been assumed, perhaps cynically, that Shipment comes just as player numbers start falling off. As one of the series' most popular maps, the thinking is that bringing it back attracts a cohort of the audience who only play that map. It's often used to level up guns, and help get player levels up since the kill count is usually higher than in other, larger maps.

Indeed, Shipment typically releases alongside a dedicated, 24/7 playlist, meaning you don't have to hope for it to show up in the normal map rotation. Infinity Ward didn't say whether we can expect the same playlist this time around, though it is likely.

As with each new iteration, Modern Warfare 4 Shipment features the classic layout but in an entirely new environment inspired by locations from the game. This version has a more urban landscape look that takes after the very first version's muted colours, with Soviet-era concrete buildings in the background. The action takes place in a shipping yard by the harbour, among shipping containers, hence the name.

Incidentally, Modern Warfare 4 is also starting its first season early, with Season One kicking off 6th November, just two weeks after the game's launch, though it is curious Infinity Ward didn't wait until the season's launch to drop the map.

title: “Wild Horse Nine” Gets Lost on Easter Island
author: @NewYorker
content:
The first time John Malkovich played a killer trained by the C.I.A., he was a man of many disguises, elusive and unpredictable as the wind. The film was “In the Line of Fire” (1993), and his character, nicknamed Booth, was a psychotically disgruntled agency alum, plotting to murder the President with a custom-built plastic gun and a bullet that he stored in a rabbit’s foot. His other weapon was his voice, at once coldly precise and dangerously soft; never before had Malkovich’s distinctly odd cadences sounded so menacing. Booth spent a lot of time on the phone, taunting a veteran Secret Service agent (Clint Eastwood) about his failure, decades earlier, to protect John F. Kennedy. “Late at night, when the demons come, do you see the rifle coming out of that window?” he drawled. “Or do you see Kennedy’s head being blown apart?”

That tragedy looms heavily, but also with an air of jokey inconsequence, over “Wild Horse Nine,” a new film written and directed by Martin McDonagh. It begins in 1973, in Santiago, Chile, where Chris Carlisle (Malkovich), a longtime C.I.A. operative, is stationed. Early on, he reminisces about the popularly elected regimes that he’s toppled, from Guatemala to Congo, and—here his voice drops to a low murmur—acknowledges a prominent role in the Kennedy assassination. Yet, despite this dabbling in POTUS-cide, Chris is something of an anti-Booth; he has too much debonair wit, too much bon-vivant style. He and his loyal protégé, Lee Chesterfield (Sam Rockwell), are headed to Easter Island for a week, and Chris, looking dandy in bright-colored neckties and a porkpie hat, has no use for disguises. As for a rabbit’s foot, forget it: Chris’s luck has run out. He’s dying of cancer and has decided that Easter Island will be his last hurrah. He wants Lee, whose marksmanship he trusts as much as his friendship, to hasten his departure.

Lee, whose frequent exasperation with Chris is a sure sign of love, has his own problems back home in the U.S., chiefly a “drunk wife who fucks clowns.” That’s Chris’s odd, harsh appraisal, and it is repeated, mirthlessly, when we finally meet said wife (Parker Posey), badgering Lee over the phone. Whenever McDonagh hits a stale comic patch like this, he retreats swiftly into the trappings of plot: Lee is understandably less than thrilled about Chris’s instant-death wish, but, by all appearances, M.J. (a cranky Steve Buscemi), the C.I.A.’s South American bureau chief, already has a finger on the trigger. Chris, often strung out on morphine, his memory and his wits addled by cancer, has become a jaw-flapping liability.

Despite the far-flung setting and the spy-thriller machinations, then, we are in terrain that McDonagh knows all too well: the bloody buddy comedy. Like his film “In Bruges” (2008), “Wild Horse Nine” follows two hit men on holiday, and, like “The Banshees of Inisherin” (2022), it conjures the verdant magic of a remote island setting. Yet the flavor of the proceedings is markedly different. In “Inisherin,” a bitter clash between two friends, played by Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson (who both also starred in “In Bruges”), felt exquisitely of a piece with the local elements: the mists, the jagged rocks, the salty tang of the sea. The outdoors lent a wry, soulful grandeur to the characters’ expletive-riddled bickering.

There are profanities aplenty in “Wild Horse Nine,” as there are in all McDonagh’s movies and plays. (Cut out the F-bombs and most of them would run barely an hour.) And the vast expanse of Easter Island, majestically filmed by the cinematographer Ben Davis, is astonishing to behold. (Lee himself can’t resist filming with a Super 8 camera, and his grainy images add welcome blips of texture.) Feral horses roam the landscape, and they give the movie both its title and its desired genre: McDonagh strives for the laconic sweep of a classic Western. But not all material can command a space this vast, and I suspect that John Ford himself might have struggled to wring much poetry from Chris and Lee, two ugly-American blowhards wisecracking their way around paradise. Really, the shenanigans could have been transplanted anywhere: picture two guys farting at Stonehenge for an hour or two, only to realize, like the ancients before them, that it makes an awfully nice burial ground.

Within such comedic confines, and with a surprising dearth of violent mayhem, “Wild Horse Nine” strains for thematic expansiveness. Ostensibly, the film is about the mixed blessings of friendship, the soul-corroding nature of violence, the horrors of U.S. foreign policy, the possibility of redemption, and the inescapability of death. But it’s the stiffest, least cohesive film on those subjects you could imagine. McDonagh organizes his scenes into thematic blocks, and whenever he loses interest in one block he simply switches, mechanically, to the next. The conversations that he’s written for Chris and Lee toggle between humor and pathos, between self-satisfied snark and self-conscious elegy, and there’s barely a moment when you don’t hear the grinding of tonal gears. (You hear it in the music, too; the Rolling Stones’ “Out of Time” isn’t the subtlest of needle drops.)

McDonagh’s dialogue is famed for its staccato crackle, but here he slows the characters’ rhythms, as if to accommodate the diminution of Chris’s body and mind, and packs dead air around everyone’s lines. Yet within those rhythms Malkovich does locate odd, narcotized flashes of poetry. His voice is lower and shakier than usual, and the gleam in his eyes sometimes goes ambiguously dull: are Chris’s mental lapses real, or part of some long con? Chris hasn’t lost his saucy erudition; one of his funnier bits is a mid-breakfast monologue on why “gay countries,” like France, produce the highest-quality cheeses. But he seems on precarious ground, no longer certain of his punch lines. He is also rediscovering the guilt and terror of his Catholic upbringing, and he wonders if, after a life spent overthrowing democracies—the coup that will depose President Salvador Allende is in the offing—he has a chance in hell of entering Heaven.

Easter Island is, of course, dotted with towering volcanic-stone figures with large, elongated faces. Chris and Lee refer to them as “the big heads,” and when a tourist couple gently note that the Indigenous term is “moai,” Lee erupts in fury—though Rockwell, who’s good at modulating an explosion, makes clear that Lee is exaggerating his rage for Chris’s benefit. Earlier, at the Santiago airport, they had an awkward run-in with two Chilean college students, Monica (Mariana di Girolamo) and Alicia (Ailín Salas), one of whom explained that the Indigenous name for Easter Island is Rapa Nui. “You shouldn’t even know the word ‘Indigenous’ at your age,” Chris replied.

It’s telling that McDonagh hammers the word “Indigenous” repeatedly and contemptuously—as opposed to, say, “local” or “Polynesian.” Back in the seventies, the term was less prevalent in English than it is today, but McDonagh, not for the first time, is eager to mock the language of the contemporary liberal scold. Farrell’s “In Bruges” character wasted no opportunity to call a dwarf a midget; in “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” (2017), McDonagh’s most pugnacious and polarizing work, Rockwell played a racist cop, annoyed that “persons of color” had replaced his favorite epithet. You could argue, I suppose, that a film shouldn’t be reduced to its characters’ politics. But, by now, it’s hard to assume that these smug linguistic sensitivities—wielded only, of course, in response to other people’s smug linguistic sensitivities—belong to anyone other than McDonagh himself. And they speak to the narrow view that he takes of his chosen setting and the harrowing historical episode into which he’s seen fit to shoehorn his characters.

“Three Billboards” hinged on the racist cop’s reformation, and “Wild Horse Nine,” with less outrageousness and more finesse, undertakes its own dubiously reconstructive exercise. Despite its misanthropic pose, the film wants very badly for us to like and even love Chris, to find him as charming as he is cancel-worthy. Chris regards his role in the deaths and disappearances of thousands of innocents with a weary shrug—and, on rare dark nights of the soul, a piddling note of regret. At one point, he notes his incongruous fondness for the local insects. “Sometimes I feel like I care more about the moths of Chile,” he says, “than I do about the people of Chile.”

McDonagh grants us a touristic view of Chile masquerading as a geopolitical one, and his dramatic aims are as obvious and limited as his emotional agenda. We’re meant to find Chris pitiable because of his diagnosis, and we’re meant to find him redeemable when he offers sincere advice to the naïvely idealistic Monica, warning her of the forthcoming horrors of the Pinochet regime. The final passages of “Wild Horse Nine” are at once swift and interminable, the action-thriller elements snapping into place at last, only to be hijacked by an exceedingly long goodbye. You can’t accuse McDonagh of not knowing his priorities; we are to shed bountiful tears for Chris, with perhaps a few to spare for his collateral damage. Some of us may be forgiven for resisting the invitation. I remained dry of eye—and rooted for the cancer. ♦

title: How a Sick Chicken Revolutionized Cancer Research - Nautilus
content:
Viruses can cause cancer. It’s something that’s well-established now, but the discovery was initially dismissed by the scientific community. Now, a new review published in Genes & Cancer is telling the story of the man responsible: Francis Peyton Rous. 

Rous was working at the Rockefeller Institute studying cancer in 1909 when a chicken farmer brought in a Barred Plymouth Rock hen with a large tumor on its breast. Unbeknownst to either of them (and especially the chicken), they would forever alter the field of cancer research. 

Read more: “A Look at How Many Cancers Are Caused by Infections Worldwide”

After examining the tumor, Rous determined it was a spindle-cell sarcoma resulting from an aggressive connective tissue cancer. By transferring cells to other chickens, Rous demonstrated the cancer could be transmitted as well—but only among chickens closely related to the afflicted bird. He also found that with each transmission, the cancer grew more malignant.  

To better understand what exactly was being passed on, Rous performed a simple experiment. He ground up the tumor tissue, extracted and filtered the fluid components, and injected cell-free solution into healthy birds. Curiously, these birds also developed tumors. Cancer, it seemed, was transmissible—and by something smaller than bacterium. The infectious agent in question was a virus, but without the molecular techniques and technology to investigate further, Rous pegged the carcinogenic culprit as a “minute parasitic organism.” (Viruses had only been discovered a couple decades prior, and weren’t well understood.)

The discovery would later prove to be “one of the foundational paradigm-shifts in 20th-century oncology,” as the researchers wrote, but it wouldn’t be properly recognized for decades. Instead, Rous’s findings were either questioned, downplayed, or discarded as inconsequential to human physiology. Cancer, it was believed, resulted from abnormalities in the cells.  

It would take more than half a century for Rous’s discoveries to receive their appropriate acclaim. In the 1950s, advances in both virology and cell culture techniques revealed the transformational properties of the Rous-sarcoma virus. Not long after, the virus helped shed light on the genetic machinery of cancer, demonstrating how proto-oncogenes can turn into oncogenes, causing unchecked cell growth.

Rous received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1966. Since then, scientists have identified a slew of viruses capable of causing cancer in humans, including human papilloma virus, Epstein–Barr virus, hepatitis B, and many more.

“What began with the investigation of a tumor-bearing chicken at the Rockefeller Institute therefore contributed to a chain of discoveries that profoundly changed our understanding of cancer biology and its molecular basis,” the researchers concluded.

title: Defending the Midterms from Donald Trump
author: @NewYorker
content:
The reporter Barton Gellman discusses threats to the upcoming elections.

October 30, 2026

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up for our daily newsletter to get the best of The New Yorker in your inbox.

Amid all the prognostication about which party will emerge triumphant during the midterms, there has also been increasing alarm: Will it be a free and fair election? As soon as Donald Trump returned to office, he began making moves to create disruption—demanding private voter data from states, threatening election officials with jail time, and even seizing ballots from prior elections to investigate alleged fraud. And although, so far, none of the White House’s efforts have threatened to significantly alter the results, the Department of Justice has hinted that there is more to come. The U.S. Attorney General, Todd Blanche, has not ruled out using the force of law to prevent election certifications. Furthermore, a lawsuit from the Trump Administration against the State of Alaska is already under way, before a single vote has even been counted. The reporter Barton Gellman and David Remnick discuss the threats to the midterm elections and Gellman’s new piece, “The State Officials Defending the Midterms from the President.”

Further reading:

  • “How ICE Is Targeting the 2026 Midterms,” by Jonathan Blitzer
  • “What the Gerrymandering Wars Mean for the Midterms—and 2028,” by Isaac Chotiner
  • “The G.O.P.’s Latest Voter-Suppression Plan,” by Sue Halpern
  • “Donald Trump Already Knows the 2026 Election Is ‘Rigged,’ ” by Susan B. Glasser

title: A Global Anti-Right Backlash
author: @NewYorker
content:
On a hazy Monday morning in Chandigarh, a city in northern India, Anish Gawande woke up early to check the news he had fallen asleep waiting for. Some nine thousand miles and eight time zones away, Brazil’s President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had emerged the winner of his country’s Presidential runoff, a victory that two weeks earlier had seemed improbable. But the left-wing incumbent defied the polls and the prediction markets, mounted a campaign that turned tens of thousands out into the streets, mobilized countless more through social-media apps, and pulled in millions of voters who had not cast their ballot for him in the first round, earlier in the month. Lula’s comeback was inspiring to Gawande, a national spokesperson of one of India’s opposition parties and a voluble critic, on the evening news shows and social media, of the right-wing Hindu-nationalist government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In 2020, Gawande had protested the Modi government’s hosting of Brazil’s then President, Jair Bolsonaro—the convicted coup-plotting father of Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right challenger whom Lula defeated Sunday—as India’s chief guest for its annual Republic Day commemorations. Bolsonaro’s documented homophobia and his acceleration of the deforestation of the Amazon rain forest seemed, to Gawande, an echo of the divisive, destructive politics of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

In recent months, Gawande has supported and defended the Gen Z uprising that has rocked Modi’s rule, with authorities unable to stamp out rolling protests in New Delhi and other Indian cities. The mass demonstrations, Gawande told me, have “revived the space for dissent in the country,” amid widespread anger over both an economy that has failed to create enough jobs for India’s huge population of young people and an increasingly autocratic politics where more than a hundred and thirty million people have been knocked off voter rolls on dubious grounds. Gawande saw a lesson in Lula’s ability to rally a diverse coalition of movements and parties in the perceived defense of Brazilian democracy. “What Lula’s victory demonstrates is that perhaps it is possible to craft solidarities between these movements, to assemble a rainbow coalition that can take on the might of Modi’s B.J.P.,” Gawande told me. He posted on Instagram, “If it happened in Brazil, it can happen in India.”

In this optimism, Gawande was joined by politicians far afield. After years of gloom in the shadow of President Donald Trump, Modi, Bolsonaro, and others of their ilk, progressives and liberals around the world are finding cause to celebrate. The center-left Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, who has called a snap election in the coming weeks against an emboldened right, declared, “What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain,” adding, “The comeback of global progressivism has just begun.” Dominique de Villepin, a former French Prime Minister, said that Lula’s victory is “a major signal of hope,” even for France, where the far right is favored to win power in the Presidential elections next year, and where mass protests continue around the country. “The democrats have won the first round of a grand global referendum on democracy,” he wrote on X about Lula’s win.

Like the triumphalism of many from the West’s far right in earlier election cycles, such enthusiasm may be short-lived, a moment of transcendence soon to be subsumed by the churn of polarization and the sclerosis of daily politics. Sánchez’s plans on keeping his job hinge on, at best, cobbling together enough votes to form a stronger coalition than the minority government he currently leads. In India, the B.J.P. retains outsized control over the apparatus of state, the media, and the courts. In Brazil, inflation is high and public debt is surging, and the legislature and state governments are dominated by Lula’s opponents. But his win has blocked what seemed an inexorable advance of the right across Latin America, where left-leaning governments have fallen in rapid succession over the past two years, and has thwarted the Bolsonaros’ broader project of judicial overhaul at home and the potential yoking of Brazil’s foreign policy to Trump’s hemispheric agenda. Ahead of the runoff, Lula cast himself as the defender of Brazilian sovereignty from the predations of Washington and U.S. tech giants, and as the ally of working people against callous élites—he didn’t shy away from his own brand of populism. In the election’s aftermath, Bolsonaro briefly attempted to claim that the result was illegitimate, but he saw right-wing heads of state in South America recognize Lula’s victory. On Wednesday, Bolsonaro, who is under investigation for corruption, money laundering, and tax evasion, for accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced financier to produce a movie about his father, landed in Miami after fleeing Brazil. (Bolsonaro has not been formally charged and has denied any wrongdoing.)

Between the defeat of Bolsonaro this past week and events earlier this year in Hungary, where the long-ruling nationalist Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted in elections, the White House has lost two hugely symbolic allies in its broader right-wing global culture war. By Wednesday, no clear winner had emerged in the Israeli election, in which Trump had endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and which saw a historic turnout of Arab voters. And the U.S. President may be humbled further in next week’s midterms, as Democrats eye taking both the House and the Senate. Former President Barack Obama, while stumping for Democrats in Ohio, blasted the Republicans in terms that would have been familiar in Brazil and elsewhere, pointing to the wealthy élites and tech titans who “are able to buy and sell elections like never before,” in service of a Republican Party that “now seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government.”

Lula withstood an anti-incumbency challenge on the same day that another once indomitable leader succumbed to one. The Serbian President, Aleksandar Vučić, a close Orbán ally, an erstwhile friend of the Kremlin, and a right-wing strongman effectively in power since 2012, saw his bid to stay in office by running to be Prime Minister foiled by an upstart student movement. The slate of candidates from its de-facto party, called the Student List, outperformed Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party, and he conceded. The students had been protesting since 2024, when the deadly collapse of a canopy outside a train station in the city of Novi Sad triggered a revolt over perceived state corruption and mismanagement. The protests, which were met at times with sweeping police repression, were resilient, and morphed into a strategic political project that persevered in the face of Vučić’s tactics, which included using state-media channels to tar the students as foreign stooges abetting a deep-state globalist agenda. Now they are trying to figure out how to form the next government in Belgrade, and, like Orbán’s opponents in Hungary, they have embarked on a campaign to reinforce the rule of law in the country and to purge state institutions of those who enabled their autocratic capture.

Those efforts are being mirrored elsewhere. “The vision of Serbian youth converges with that of many other young Europeans,” Nathalie Tocci, an Italian political scientist and former foreign-policy adviser to top E.U. officials, wrote in La Stampa. She pointed to the series of protests convulsing the Continent: there’s the Flamingo movement in Albania—where demonstrations have pulled in a cross-section of society, including students and professionals, infuriated by the government’s handling of a project backed by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner to open a luxury resort along a coastal ecological preserve, and have surfaced wider public rage against oligarchs in the country. And then there are those who have marched in recent weeks in France, Belgium, Spain, and Italy, calling for access to affordable housing, relief with the cost of living, and greater investment in their schools. “It is a vision of democracy, equality, and social, environmental, international, and intergenerational justice,” Tocci added. “A vision and a commitment expressed through street protests.”

Of course, that’s not the universal view of the unrest. In the chaotic recent scenes from Paris and other French cities, in particular, members of the American and European right have sought confirmation for their culture-war talking points, laying the blame for the vandalism, fires on the boulevards, and looting on Muslim migrants and the alleged leftist extremists who appease them. Online, some Republicans and their supporters linked the chaos to the supposedly globalist world view of Democrats, invoking the spectral menace of communists and jihadists storming through the West’s fallen capitals. But that hysteria misses deeper realities, including the entrenched traditions of confrontational protest in France.

Political Islam has nothing to do with these protests. The unrest began with students unhappy about conditions in their schools and universities, but ballooned into something far larger, activating a swathe of French society that reviles the perceived neoliberalism of President Emmanuel Macron and wants to see greater public investment. It also pulled in apolitical opportunists who participated in the looting, while the government blamed the “ultra left.” Like the Gen Z protests in New Delhi earlier this summer, the protests, which were largely peaceful, were met at times with a crushing police response. Yet some observers have warned that the actions of a minority of the crowd—ransacking businesses and an arson attack that gutted the town hall of Limoges—may be strengthening the hand of the far-right leader Marine Le Pen. Macron is profoundly unpopular, complicating the path for a centrist successor next year. The protesters see their revolutionary zeal as offering a kind of renewal to a flagging French republic—one of their slogans is “On refait 1789 pour ne pas revenir en 1939,” that is, “We are redoing 1789 so as not to return to 1939.” Whether a majority of French voters will be persuaded by the spectacle of the barricades remains to be seen.

There’s no simple narrative bringing together all the separate uprisings. “They are dispersed points of resonance that still need to be tuned to one another,” the Belgian philosopher Michel Feher told an interviewer. Sánchez, in Spain, called the snap election when his ruling coalition was unable to pass housing legislation that many Spaniards had been demanding. In India, anger over the administration of school-board exams snowballed into a larger rebellion against Modi’s illiberal, majoritarian rule. But Matthew Cebul, a researcher on nonviolent resistance movements at the Harvard Kennedy School, sees all these protests as rooted in a universal desire for accountability from one’s government and rage at perceived graft and cronyism. “Illiberal governments thrive on this aura of inevitability or perceived social dominance, but illiberalism is ultimately hollow and vulnerable, especially when it performs poorly,” Cebul told me. He added, “People do not like being governed by crooks and thugs. They want competent governance, not arrogant corruption, and democracy movements can and are winning people over when they call for something better.” ♦

title: Why a world without friction is a world without progress | Aeon Essays
content:
In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to be that decreasing resistance makes life easier and smoother.

Having spent a career as a tribologist, studying friction, wear and lubrication scientifically, I have some opinions on this. I’ll confess that, in most of my career, I too have sought to reduce friction, developing new materials, designs or even instrumentation in order to lower friction in a jet engine or reduce emissions from your car. However, I’ve also found myself trying to figure out how to increase friction to remove plaque on teeth.

The reality is that friction, despite seeming so antagonistic, is necessary and even productive. The force that resists motion has, since humans first struck a spark from a stone, been the very thing that propels us forward. And this paradox offers a lens through which to reread humanity’s entire technological history.

In order to appreciate all that an understanding of friction has helped us to accomplish, it’s necessary to start at square one and state what friction actually is. We define friction as the force that resists motion, and that means friction is rather ubiquitous. If things are moving, whether they’re sliding around or rolling, there’s friction. Solids, liquids, gases? Doesn’t matter. If there’s movement, friction is there to resist it. Unfortunately, because friction’s job is to resist, we’ve developed an aversion to it as a nuisance. But it’s a very important force, and we’ve thrived by expanding our understanding of it. By the 1960s, after millennia of evolving with friction, we finally accepted that friction is such a critical part of our world that a scientific field of study needed to be devoted to it: tribology.

Tribologists like me study this force in all its forms. Tribology is the science of interacting surfaces in relative motion, concerned with the wear of materials, friction and lubrication. Basically, tribology is the specialisation of things rubbing against each other. You may raise an eyebrow at a field of science focused on this, but when you pause to consider how much motion is going on inside us, around us and throughout the Universe, you can appreciate that tribology is vast. More than anyone, tribologists know the problems friction can cause. But they also know the achievements that have followed as we’ve come to understand resistance better.

Although tribology as a formalised field is relatively modern, friction has long shaped humanity’s technological innovations. For example, consider its pivotal role in people’s journeys from A to B over the centuries. I’m willing to bet that whenever you need to move unwieldy furniture or carry home that giant bag of cat litter, your instinct is to find a cart to help you. Early humans had a similar thought, turning to log rollers to move heavy objects, and coming up with one of our greatest inventions: the wheel. Rolling makes it easier to move objects because it reduces friction between the object and surface you’re moving it against. There are far fewer surface interactions in the process of rolling versus sliding. Plenty can be said about the wheel, including the fact that even in 2026 we can’t seem to agree on the origin of its discovery, but there is zero doubt that it’s a brilliant innovation for dealing with friction. But wheels also need friction: when we exert a force to move a wheel forward, the force between the ground and the wheel – static friction – keeps it from spinning freely, which would result in us going nowhere. Once forward motion begins, the resistance to motion becomes dynamic friction, which is just as important. If you’ve driven on ice, you know the danger of too little friction.

However, if people hadn’t continued improving on these basic principles, even the wheel would be rather inefficient due to friction.

The Vikings’ longships minimised form drag so they could cut through the water quickly

The ancient Romans discovered this in their amphitheatres. Roman chariot races didn’t come without their headaches. Or rather, foot aches. I’m certain the drivers likely complained about their hot feet, caused by friction between the wheels and axle heating up the surrounding parts. In Odes, a collection of lyric poems, the poet Horace described how chariot wheels would glow during racing. Today, scientists know that this glow is from turning the energy of motion into thermal energy. Roman designers eventually figured out that they could temper the problem by putting axungia (animal fat) grease between the wheel and axle. By doing so, they were applying tribological knowledge already exploited by the Sumerians: that fats and oils work more effectively than water as lubrication between surfaces. However, that created a new conundrum: if the grease got hot enough, it risked catching fire. The solution? A coolant. In this case, they splashed water on the chariots, in the ancient equivalent of a pit stop.

While all roads led to Rome, you could say all seas led to the Vikings. They, too, cleverly adapted to the resistance that met them as they journeyed through the oceans. Moving through fluids produces a type of friction known as drag. Even within drag there are subsets. Skin drag is from the friction between the surface of the ship and the water, whereas form drag stems from the shape of the hull as it moves through the water. When they had to transport cargo safely, the Vikings used sturdy ships with wide hulls. This wider hull increased form drag and slowed them down, but the stability provided was more critical. Their famous longships, however, were long and slim, minimising form drag as much as possible so they could cut through the water quickly.

As with all friction scenarios, however, the Vikings found themselves having to balance some competing demands. Faster longships are better, yes, but it was also imperative that the ships not break apart into pieces from the waves. They needed flexibility and strength, while keeping the ships as light as possible to ride higher in the water to reduce drag. To do this, the Vikings used their ‘clinker’ technique of nailing together long planks of wood. The rivets and overlapping planks would increase drag compared with a more polished, smoother design but these individual planks gave the ships the ability to twist and flex to weather storms. If I was on a boat trip in the middle of the ocean, I too would be happy to sacrifice a little bit of drag reduction to avoid capsizing from a rogue wave.

Looking at boats and ships today, it’s clear that we didn’t just accept these Viking designs as the culmination of nautical perfection. Likewise, we aren’t driving around in Roman chariots today. We have since made incredible leaps forward in understanding how to quantify friction and thus design for it, finally approaching friction scientifically. In the 1920s, Chrysler’s head of engineering Carl Breer had the idea to design cars with aerodynamics in mind. Planes seemed to slice seamlessly through the air. Shouldn’t cars do the same? Breer tasked the engineer William Earnshaw to consult with none other than Orville Wright to learn how to design a car in a wind tunnel. The resulting teardrop-shaped Chrysler Airflow was considered a flop, as many disruptive designs can be when they’re just too jarring for taste, but that flop revolutionised how we design cars. Wind-tunnel testing remains a standard today, and friction’s presence is as expected as the air itself.

Tribology testing is routine for the automotive industry today, and there are tribology labs scattered throughout a variety of industries, from medical to food. In these labs, you’ll find instruments designed to measure friction at macro-scales down to the atomic level. My PhD lab at the University of Florida had tribometers measuring friction in force ranges that covered three orders of magnitude. I’ve even worked in a lab that had a tribometer built to test an actual train wheel against a railway. Tribologists are incredibly clever with innovating ways to measure friction, given how persnickety friction is. Friction is dependent on the conditions of the operation – how fast things are moving, how much force they experience, and what temperature and environment they’re in.

Temperature in particular is a fun variable to contend with, because friction itself leads to temperature changes; indeed, frictional heating can be extreme in some cases. Like with Roman chariots, greases can ignite at certain temperatures making it imperative to control friction heating in order to avoid accidentally reaching that temperature. And for applications like jet engines, which get very hot anyway, we have engineered solid materials with low friction to withstand the heat.

When tribologists run into a wall, we develop a new instrument to understand what friction is trying to tell us

You may think tribology is already a niche field, but we have specialisations within it. Mine was solid lubrication, and I worked on developing and testing materials for jet engines and automobiles. In some cases, the conditions of the end use were so aggressive that the steel I was running my material against would experience enough friction heating to completely change the colour of the steel. That’s how you know you’ve reached the extremes in tribology, but those extremes must be met and they obviously are. After all, we have space stations orbiting Earth and landers on Mars.

Which brings us to another critical point about friction’s role in human progress: resistance is a consequence of progress, and its existence is a sign of progression itself. We wouldn’t have the now-robust business of solid lubricants if we had not advanced technologically to design turbine engines, which themselves were the result of us figuring out powered flight. By achieving that, our progress led us to new resistance. I think this is critical to remember anytime we find ourselves confronting unexpected resistance, and it’s something I remind myself of whenever I get halted in my work. I wouldn’t be stumped by this new resistance if I hadn’t managed to advance myself to this position where the resistance exists.

Often when tribologists run into a wall, we find ourselves developing a new instrument to help us understand what friction is trying to tell us. Tribometers have been designed to mimic all of the variables mentioned above, and that alone is quite a feat of human engineering, but now we also couple them with other techniques that allow us to somehow see what is happening while it’s happening. From maps of frictional heating during operation to how friction is influencing cellular movement, instruments and techniques have enabled us to usher friction into a new era to drive us forward, doing more than just finding clever ways to overcome friction. We can harness it as a tool.

In terms of friction, the 20th century can be thought of as the century in which humans accepted the resistance, and established engineering rigour around friction to propel our technological advances forward. Critically, it’s when we formalised how to overcome friction to be more efficient. As a tribologist, however, I’m far more excited about what the 21st century has brought us. Instead of just overcoming friction, we began fully realising how to harness that resistance to bring in a new era of progress. Exhibit A is once again found in our cars, where friction has been deployed as a tool in sustainability. Braking requires friction, so engineers asked: why don’t we use the consequences of that friction to our advantage? The heat from friction in braking is now used to create electricity in regenerative braking in EVs and hybrids. We must continue to use this creative and fresh perspective when dealing with friction, as opposed to always driving towards frictionlessness. Imagine if those engineers had been so fixated on the negatives of friction that they didn’t harness its power.

Using friction as a tool has come to us only as we’ve evolved to understand the depths of friction, including its behaviours and where it may be lurking. We know it is involved in dynamic processes, so let’s use it to control such processes. Yes, we’ve done so for a while with mechanisms like brakes and dampeners, but expanding this beyond machines has really taken hold in recent decades. Now, we’re looking at how friction may be a tool in perhaps the most impressive machine there is: the human body. It’s possible friction may be a lever to help us better model and understand biological processes and, in turn, help in the development of therapeutics. The rate at which a virus ejects from its protein shell or capsid can dictate whether it results in an active infection or instead remains dormant in the cell. If we want to use viruses to intentionally infect and defeat other viruses or bacteria, then controlling the virus’s ejection rate is crucial. Friction is the key to unlocking this possibility. In 2023, researchers found that, by packing the coils of virus DNA in certain ways, they could increase friction during ejection and slow down its rate of ejection.

Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another

Recently, our knowledge of friction has taken us to even more surprising places, extending even to helping us understand dark matter. The concept of ‘resistance is your reward for progress’ may be best illustrated by the astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Despite the fact that established scientists mocked his theories, Chandrasekhar would go on to become a founder of astrophysics, and is the reason we understand the evolution of stars and interstellar dynamics. In the 1930s, he was interested in how the interactions between stars could lead to their collisions. He calculated the timescales of such collisions and realised, though only after publishing, that things weren’t adding up quite right. This led him back to the drawing board, where he spotted there was a resistance present that no one before had identified: dynamical friction. This friction is a gravitationally induced drag that acts on objects as they interact and move through space.

Fast-forward to the 21st century, and dynamical friction has been used as a tool to infer the presence of dark matter. In 2024, researchers in Hong Kong realised that orbital times weren’t matching up with a couple of stars they were studying that were believed to be circling around black holes. They looked at Chandrasekhar’s concept of dynamical friction and wondered what would happen if they incorporated the contribution of friction from the dark matter surrounding the black hole. Voila! Suddenly, the predicted and calculated orbital times of the stars matched with what they were measuring. Friction was present when humanity first started experimenting with fire and the wheel. Now it’s there as we probe the frontiers of our Universe.

We need friction to move. Without its resistance, Earth’s plates would be in constant motion. We could not walk, or drive, or even hold objects. Understanding how to achieve what we want, in a world requiring this resistance, has been essential in our development.

Yet there is a deeper paradox at work, one that William James captured when he wrote that life is built ‘in the self-governing resistance of the ego to the world’. Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another. We step forward, and new resistance awaits. This is what progress means: that we have moved into territory that demands new understanding.

Roman engineers learned it when their chariot wheels caught fire. Chandrasekhar discovered this when his calculations didn’t add up. And we will continue to encounter resistance as we push forward.

When people speak of a frictionless world, they imagine ease. But ease without resistance is a wheel spinning in place, motion without progress.

title: The Washington Roundtable Live: The Final Stretch with David Plouffe
author: @NewYorker
content:
With the midterms nearly upon us, the political strategist assesses where things stand, and how the chips may fall.

October 30, 2026

Listen and subscribe: Apple | Spotify | Wherever You Listen

Sign up to receive our twice-weekly News & Politics newsletter.

The Washington Roundtable is joined onstage at The New Yorker Festival by David Plouffe, the political strategist and the campaign manager for Barack Obama’s historic 2008 Presidential run, for a final look at the midterms map. With Donald Trump’s approval ratings near historic lows and fuel prices squeezing rural voters, Democrats find themselves competitive in Senate races in Iowa, Nebraska, Texas, and even Kansas, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since the nineteen-thirties. Plouffe compares these midterms to the wave elections of 1994 and 2006, and argues that Republican spending, including Elon Musk’s, can do little to stave off voter anger about the cost of living. He also looks forward to 2028, and encourages future candidates to study those who overperform this midterm cycle. “Democrats have the opportunity to make an adjustment between now and ’28. Republicans don’t,” Plouffe says. “It’s a political gift of epic proportions—if we find a way to seize it.”

title: Men Who Eat More Plant-Based Protein Have Higher Testosterone Levels - Nautilus
content:
There’s a testosterone crisis in America—at least according to a number of Trump administration officials. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., for example, has bemoaned the low-T of the American youth, and even boosts his own levels with testosterone replacement therapy. He’s also a major proponent of eating animals, celebrating the prominent position of meat and dairy in the new food pyramid the US Department of Agriculture unveiled at the beginning of this year.

But a study published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition suggests Kennedy might be able to ease up on the testosterone shots if he ate more vegetables.

A team of nutritional and metabolic scientists analyzed the four-day dietary intake and hormone levels of more than 2,500 middle-aged men living in Finland. It’s worth noting that the data in their study were also middle-aged, collected during the Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study between 1984 and 1989.

Read more: “The Impossible Strength of the Testosterone Myth”

After dividing the men into four groups according to their protein intake and controlling for other variables, the researchers found that the subjects’ testosterone levels seemed to be linked to the kind of protein they preferred. On average, the men who ate more meat and dairy had slightly lower testosterone levels. In contrast, those who got more of their protein from plant-based sources had slightly higher levels of the sex hormone. The scientists observed a similar dynamic with their levels of sex hormone binding globulin, a protein that controls how much free testosterone is available in the blood stream.

Drilling down into the dietary data, the team discovered dairy was most responsible for the relatively low-T in the animal protein group. The plant protein group’s higher testosterone levels showed a closer association with protein from vegetables, rather than cereals.

The researchers said they aren’t entirely sure why the protein source appears to affect male sex hormone levels, but said the pattern may be mediated by inflammation. Higher levels of C-reactive protein, a molecule involved in inflammatory pathways, have been linked to reduced overall testosterone levels and those who eat more plant protein typically have lower levels of C-reactive protein.

Additionally, while the researchers controlled for a number of health and lifestyle variables, it’s possible that the plant-eating group had healthier habits overall. But because this is a cross-sectional observational study, causation is impossible to pin down.

Of course, there are plenty of other reasons to limit meat intake—both for your own health and the planet’s. In fact, a new international food pyramid released this week recommends getting the bulk of your calories from plants instead of animals. Testosterone-maxxing might just be an attractive bonus.

title: Death by a Thousand Dams
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Thousands of small, often obsolete dams are blocking fish migrations across the United States. In this piece, Ben Goldfarb explores the growing movement to remove these barriers—despite political, economic, and emotional obstacles. He asks, “Can government agencies and conservation groups pick up the pace of dam removal while fish are still around to benefit?”

The Eastern Seaboard’s most enthusiastic purger of dams has long been Plymouth, Massachusetts, and one weekend I visited during its Herring Festival, a celebration of the resurgent alewife population that annually runs up Town Brook, the stream at Plymouth’s heart. The day was cool and damp, and I followed a posse of dads in Red Sox sweatshirts and kids in rainboots up the path that paralleled the creek. Someone had chalked “LOOK FISH” on the asphalt, and I glanced streamward to find alewives holding in small pods, weaving around each other in their effortless way.
